questions.question: What does LPG stand for in the context of India's economic reforms?

• LPG reforms were introduced in **1991** to address the economic crisis faced by India.
 
• **Liberalisation** refers to the relaxation of previous government restrictions in areas such as trade and industry.
 
• **Privatisation** involves transferring ownership of businesses from the public sector to the private sector.
 
• **Globalisation** signifies the integration of the Indian economy with the global economy through trade, investment, and technology.
 
• These reforms aimed at **improving efficiency, productivity, and competitiveness** in the Indian economy.

• It includes measures such as reducing tariffs, lifting export-import restrictions, and deregulating industries.
 
• Focuses on **free-market policies** to stimulate economic growth.
 
• Encourages **foreign direct investment (FDI)** to boost capital inflow.
 
 
 
• **Privatisation**
 
 
• Aims to **reduce the fiscal burden** on the government by selling state-owned enterprises.
 
• Enhances **efficiency** by introducing market-driven management practices.
 
• Promotes **competition** and consumer choice.
 
 
 
• **Globalisation**
 
 
• Encourages **international trade** and investment.
 
• Facilitates the **transfer of technology** and innovation.

• These reforms included measures such as deregulation, reduction of import tariffs, and opening up to foreign investments.
 
• The primary focus was on increasing productivity and efficiency through competition and global engagement.
 
• Key sectors targeted included industrial policy, trade policy, and financial sector reforms.
 
• The reforms marked a significant shift from a closed, centrally planned economy to a market-driven one.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes globalisation?
questions.solution:
The Correct answer is __**Increasing international interdependence and trade**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Globalisation** refers to the process of increasing worldwide **interdependence** among economies, cultures, and populations due to **international trade, technology, investment, and cultural exchange.**
 
• It leads to the integration of **global markets**, fostering the movement of goods, services, capital, and labor across borders.
 
• Globalisation promotes economic growth by creating access to **larger markets** and encouraging **competition**, which drives innovation and efficiency.
 
• It enhances cultural exchange, enabling the dissemination of **ideas, traditions, and knowledge** across the globe.
 
• International organisations like the **World Trade Organization (WTO)** and agreements such as **Free Trade Agreements (FTAs)** play a significant role in facilitating globalisation.
 
• Major drivers of globalisation include advancements in **technology**, such as the internet, and improvements in **transportation infrastructure**, which reduce barriers to trade and communication.
 
• Globalisation has also led to the rise of **multinational corporations**, which operate in multiple countries and contribute to the interconnectedness of economies.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Isolating economies from global markets**__

 __
 
• This option describes the opposite of globalisation, commonly referred to as **economic isolationism**.
 
• Economic isolation involves limiting trade and interaction with other countries to protect domestic industries or maintain self-reliance.
 
• Some countries adopt isolationist policies during periods of crisis, but such measures often hinder **economic growth** and innovation.
 
 
 
• **Reducing international trade**__
 __
 
• Reducing international trade generally occurs due to **protectionist policies**, such as tariffs, quotas, and trade restrictions.
 
• This approach contrasts with globalisation, which aims to increase the exchange of goods and services across borders.
 
• While protectionism can safeguard certain industries, it may lead to reduced **economic efficiency** and less consumer choice.
 
 
 
• **Limiting cultural exchange**__
 
 
• Limiting cultural exchange is the opposite of one of the benefits of globalisation, which fosters the sharing of **traditions, languages, and practices** worldwide.
 
• Restricting cultural exchange can lead to a lack of **mutual understanding and cooperation** between nations.
 
• Globalisation enhances cultural diversity by enabling people to experience and adopt elements from other cultures.

questions.question: Which type of poverty is generally considered as a result of insufficient income?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Absolute poverty**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Absolute poverty** refers to a condition where an individual’s income is insufficient to meet the basic human needs of subsistence, including food, shelter, and clothing.
 
• It is typically defined by a fixed threshold or minimum level of income required to maintain the minimum standard of living.
 
• The World Bank defines absolute poverty as living on less than $1.90 a day, adjusted for purchasing power parity.
 
• Unlike relative poverty, absolute poverty is not concerned with income disparities between individuals or groups but focuses solely on whether basic needs are being met.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Relative Poverty**

 
 
• Relative poverty is measured in relation to the economic status of other people in society. It is concerned with inequality and social inclusion.
 
• It is often defined as having an income below a certain percentage (e.g., 50%) of the median income in a given society.
 
• This measure highlights the social dimension of poverty, where individuals or groups are considered poor if they fall significantly below the average living standards of the society they live in.
 
 
 
• **Situational Poverty**
 
 
• Situational poverty is typically a short-term condition caused by sudden and unexpected crises such as natural disasters, job loss, or health emergencies.
 
• Individuals in situational poverty may have access to resources and support systems that can help them recover.
 
 
 
• **Urban Poverty**
 
 
• Urban poverty refers to poverty found within urban areas, characterized by overcrowded living conditions, inadequate access to services, and limited employment opportunities.
 
• It often involves a lack of access to adequate housing, healthcare, and education within city environments.
 
 
 
• **Measurement of Poverty**
 
 
• Poverty can be measured using various indicators, including income levels, consumption patterns, access to essential services, and living conditions.
 
• Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI) is another measure that considers various deprivations experienced by people in their daily lives, such as poor health, lack of education, and inadequate living standards.

questions.question: Which of the following is a government programme meant to reduce poverty in India?

__
 
• NRLM, also known as Aajeevika, was launched by the Ministry of Rural Development in June 2011.
 
• The mission aims to reduce poverty by promoting self-employment and the organization of rural poor.
 
• The scheme focuses on the creation of efficient and effective institutional platforms of the rural poor.
 
• These platforms enable the poor to increase household income through sustainable livelihood enhancements and improved access to financial services.
 
• NRLM targets to reach out to 7 crore rural poor households across 600 districts, 6000 blocks, 2.5 lakh gram panchayats, and 6 lakh villages in India.

• **Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act (MGNREGA)**

 
 
• Launched in 2005, MGNREGA aims to enhance livelihood security in rural areas by providing at least 100 days of wage employment in a financial year to every household.
 
• It focuses on sustainable development by creating durable assets (such as roads, canals, ponds, and wells).
 
• The scheme ensures social inclusion by strengthening the livelihood base of rural poor.
 
• It is a demand-driven program where the provision of work is based on the demand for employment in rural areas.
 
 
 
• **Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana - Gramin (PMAY-G)**
 
 
• Launched in 2016, the scheme aims to provide a pucca house with basic amenities to all houseless householders and those living in kutcha houses by 2022.

• It ensures the construction of quality houses using local materials, designs, and technology.
 
• The scheme empowers beneficiaries by involving them in the construction process.
 
 
 
• **Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana (PMFBY)**
 
 
• Launched in 2016, PMFBY aims to provide financial support to farmers suffering crop loss/damage due to unforeseen events.
 
• It stabilizes the income of farmers and encourages them to adopt innovative and modern agricultural practices.
 
• The scheme provides a uniform premium of only 2% to be paid by farmers for all Kharif crops and 1.5% for all Rabi crops.
 
• In the case of annual commercial and horticultural crops, the premium is 5%.
 
 
 
• **National Social Assistance Programme (NSAP)**
 
 
• Launched in 1995, NSAP is a welfare program to provide financial assistance to the elderly, widows, and persons with disabilities in the form of social pensions.
 
• The scheme includes Indira Gandhi National Old Age Pension Scheme, Indira Gandhi National Widow Pension Scheme, and Indira Gandhi National Disability Pension Scheme.
 
• It is a centrally sponsored scheme funded by the Government of India and implemented by state governments.
 
• The program aims to ensure a minimum national standard for social assistance benefits.

• The **preventive **approach of HACCP-based procedures **not only improves **food safety management but also **complements **other **quality management systems**.

questions.question: Industrial Policy Resolution, 1956 was adopted in which of the following five-year plans?
questions.solution:

__
 
• The **Industrial Policy Resolution, 1956** was a significant policy document that laid the framework for industrial development in India.
 
• This resolution was adopted during the **2nd Five-Year Plan (1956-1961)**.
 
• The policy emphasized the importance of the public sector and aimed to establish a socialistic pattern of society.
 
• It categorized industries into three schedules:
 
 
• **Schedule A**: Industries exclusively owned by the state.
 
• **Schedule B**: Industries progressively state-owned, with private sector participation.
 
• **Schedule C**: Remaining industries open to the private sector.
 
 
 
• The resolution aimed to promote **rapid industrialization** and reduce **income inequalities**.
 
• It laid the foundation for subsequent industrial policies and was crucial in shaping India's industrial landscape.

 __
 
• The **3rd Five-Year Plan** (1961-1966) aimed at establishing a **self-reliant economy**.
 
• It focused on **agriculture** and **industry** with a goal to make India **self-sufficient in food grains**.
